## What I did

The requirement was that all rejections (400, 409, 429) return an RFC7807 `application/problem+json` body. Two gaps existed, each fixed as a small, self-contained unit so no large method or class had to grow:

1. **400 — `src/.../rest/validation/ValidPostcodeValidator.java`** (1 line changed). When `city` was missing, the class-level `@ValidPostcode` validator called `Locality.of(null)`, which NPE'd; Hibernate wrapped that as a `ValidationException` and it fell through to the general handler as a **500**. I added a null-city guard so the postcode check defers to the field's existing `@NotNull`, which now surfaces as a normal **400** rendered as problem+json by the existing `ExceptionControllerAdvice`. This is exactly the case the new `AcceptanceTest.coreRejectionIsProblemJson` exercises.

2. **409 / 429 — new `src/.../rest/advice/ProblemDetailResponseFilter.java`.** These statuses are returned by `addOwner` as bare `ResponseEntity`s with **empty bodies**, so no exception handler could render them. Rather than editing the large, high-complexity `addOwner` method (and its class full of other methods), I added a small `OncePerRequestFilter` that — reusing the codebase's existing `ContentCachingResponseWrapper` idiom — attaches a minimal `type`/`title`/`status`/`detail` problem document to any rejection-status response that has no body yet. It leaves the advice-rendered 400 body untouched (it only fills empty bodies).

HTTP status codes are unchanged throughout. I verified the 400 path with the provided acceptance test and separately confirmed the 409 path emits a well-formed problem+json body (temporary test since removed). Full suite: **BUILD SUCCESS**.

Structural impact stayed low: one 1-line edit to a single-method validator class (near-zero surrounding complexity) plus one new cohesive filter class with two simple methods — the large `addOwner` method and its controller were not touched.
